text: Not once did Jesus make someone sick, and not once did He eat the loaves Himself and send the crowd away hungry.
explanation:
"He who has seen Me has seen the Father." If you want to know God's will, look at Jesus. He "went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil." You'd think there'd be at least one story of Him saying, "You look too healthy; take some leprosy," or "Today it's not God's will to feed you." There isn't one.

He opened blind eyes, cleansed lepers, raised the dead, and fed thousands twice. "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever." Don't let anyone's theology convince you that God's heart toward you is anything less.

text: "Those who receive abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness will reign in life." Receive here means to seize.
explanation:
"If by the one man's offence death reigned… much more those who receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the One, Jesus Christ." Death reigns over everyone like a king; no amount of money or denial keeps it away. But grace reigns "much more."

The word for receive, lambano, is the word used when soldiers seized Jesus in Gethsemane: an active, firm taking hold. Grab hold of two things: abundant grace, and righteousness as a gift, not a reward. When you reign, sin, addiction and death don't.

text: Under grace, a lack of blessing usually isn't a lack of devotion. It's an area of unbelief.
explanation:
Under the law, when things went wrong, you looked for the commandment you broke. Under the new covenant, the issue isn't whether you've consecrated yourself enough; it's whether you've believed. "The righteous by faith shall live": the gospel reveals righteousness that comes by faith, and the power of God for your whole salvation flows through it.

In the New Testament, faith is linked to righteousness about twenty times, far more than to anything else. Its first use is to believe you're righteous when your thoughts, feelings and failures all say otherwise. That's the faith that pleases God.

text: The spirit of faith: "I believed, and therefore I spoke." David told Goliath how it would end before the stone left the sling.
explanation:
Goliath really was huge, armed and experienced. David didn't deny it. But before the battle began he declared, "This day the Lord will deliver you into my hand." Paul says we have "the same spirit of faith": we believe, and therefore we speak.

It works both ways. People who expect the worst say so: "Somebody's bound to fall sick on holiday," "Good things never happen to me," and then say, "I told you so." When God saw darkness, He didn't describe it; He said, "Light, be." Believe what God says about you, and say it.

text: God renamed Abram "father of many nations" before he had a son by Sarah. Every time someone called his name, they spoke God's promise.
explanation:
God "calls those things which do not exist as though they did." Abraham was nearly a hundred; Sarah was ninety and had always been barren. God added a letter from His own name and changed Abram (exalted father) to Abraham (father of a multitude). Imagine Sarah calling across the field, "Father of many, dinner's ready!"

Abraham "did not consider his own body, already dead," but was fully convinced God could do what He'd promised. And "by faith Sarah herself received strength to conceive." That's not denial. It's agreeing with what God already sees.

text: Christ "died to sin once for all." "Likewise," says Paul, "reckon yourself dead to sin": same manner, once for all.
explanation:
Jesus never committed a sin, so He died to the sins imputed to Him: their guilt, judgment and condemnation. Death is now behind Him forever. "Likewise you also, reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus." This is the first time Paul uses the phrase "in Christ Jesus."

Picture a pen sealed inside a Bible: wherever the Bible goes, the pen goes. God put you in Christ at the cross. When He died, you died; when He rose, you rose. "Reckon" is an accounting word: not make-believe, but counting on what's already true. You aren't dying to sin day by day. You died.

text: "Each one resembled the son of a king." The enemy recognised Gideon's brothers by their likeness to him. As He is, so are you.
explanation:
Gideon asked the captured Midianite kings what the men they'd killed at Tabor looked like. "As you are, so were they; each one resembled the son of a king." They were his brothers. Scripture goes further about you: you're a member of Christ's body, one with Him. "As He is, so are we in this world."

That's why Paul's "therefore, do not let sin reign" comes after the facts, not before. When anger or temptation rises, it doesn't define you; it's trying to bully you. You're a risen person in Christ, royalty in this world. Say it, especially when you don't feel it: "I am the righteousness of God in Christ."
